questions.question: ADT full form is ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **C) Abstract Data Type**

- **Specification vs Implementation:** An **Abstract Data Type (`ADT`)** defines a mathematical model of data values together with the **logical operations** permitted on them (e.g., `Stack` with `push`, `pop`, `peek`), completely hiding the concrete memory layout (array vs linked list).

questions.question: In a multiset, elements are arranged in an unordered manner, with elements having a multiplicity of ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) More than one**

- **Multiset (Bag) Property:** Unlike an ordinary mathematical set (where every present element has multiplicity `1`), a **multiset** is an unordered collection that permits **duplicate elements**, so present elements can have a multiplicity **more than one** (e.g., `{a, a, b}` has `m(a) = 2`).
questions.sourceNote: The legacy CST209 P002 answer was D; B is the model answer because repeat multiplicity is the defining feature of a multiset.

questions.question: Binary Search can be categorized into which of the following?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) Divide and conquer**

- **Decrease-and-Conquer Special Case:** **Binary Search** splits the sorted search interval `[low..high]` at `mid`, compares `key` with `A[mid]`, and recurses/iterates on **one half** (`T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)`), placing it under the **Divide and Conquer** paradigm.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search with iteration?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) O(log n)**

- **Halving Interval:** Each `while (low <= high)` iteration discards half of the remaining sorted elements (`n → n/2 → n/4 → … → 1`), executing at most `⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 =` **`O(log n)`** comparisons in **`O(1)`** auxiliary space.

questions.question: Which of the following is/are property/properties of a dynamic programming problem?

options.text: Both optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems

questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **D) Both optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems**

- **Two Necessary Conditions:** **Dynamic Programming** applies when global optimal solutions are built from optimal sub-solutions (**optimal substructure**) and recursive decomposition visits the **same sub-problems repeatedly** (**overlapping sub-problems**), justifying memoization/tabulation.

questions.question: A circuit that does not repeat vertices is called ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **A) a cycle**

- **Closed Walk Without Repeated Internal Vertices:** A **circuit** is a closed trail (`v₀ → v₁ → … → v_k = v₀` with no repeated edges); when **no intermediate vertices are repeated** either (`v₀, v₁, …, v_{k−1}` all distinct), it is a **(simple) cycle**.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Kruskal's algorithm (E is the number of edges and V is the number of vertices of input graph)?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) O(E log V)**

- **Sorting Dominates Runtime:** Sorting `E` edges by weight takes `O(E log E)` time, and Disjoint-Set Union-Find checks take `O(E α(V))`. Because `E ≤ V²` in a simple graph, `log E ≤ 2 log V = O(log V)`, giving **`O(E log V)`**.

questions.question: Time complexity of Insertion sort is ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) Quadratic**

- **Average & Worst-Case Growth:** On random or reverse-sorted arrays, **Insertion Sort** shifts up to `i` elements during pass `i` (`∑_{i=1}^{n−1} i = n(n−1)/2`), yielding **quadratic `Θ(n²)`** time complexity (`O(n)` linear only in the best case).
questions.sourceNote: This printed MCQ was missing from the legacy CST209 P002 partial transcription.

questions.question: If `A = {x, y, z}`, number of elements of the power set of A is ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) 8**

- **Power Set Cardinality (`|P(A)| = 2^n`):** Every element of a finite set of cardinality `n` is independently either included or excluded from a subset, producing `2^n` subsets. Here `|A| = 3`, so `|P(A)| = 2³ =` **`8`** subsets: `{∅, {x}, {y}, {z}, {x,y}, {x,z}, {y,z}, {x,y,z}}`.

questions.question: Which option contains two equal sets?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) X = {5, 6, 8, 9} and Y = {6, 8, 5, 9}**

- **Axiom of Extensionality:** Two sets are equal (`X = Y`) iff `X ⊆ Y` and `Y ⊆ X` (they contain the **exact same distinct members**, regardless of listing order). Both sets in **B** contain `{5, 6, 8, 9}`.
questions.sourceNote: Set braces and digits were visually confirmed from a zoom crop; OCR had corrupted several entries.

questions.question: Time complexity depends on ______.

options.text: both Compile time and Run time

questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) Run time**

- **Execution Step Count:** **Time complexity** quantifies how the number of elementary **run-time** operations grows as a function of dynamic input size `n`; static **compile time** does not depend on runtime input size `n`.

questions.question: Which of the following is a linear data structure?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **A) Array**

- **Sequential Organization:** An **array** arranges elements sequentially (`A[0], A[1], …, A[n−1]`) where every interior element has a unique predecessor and successor (**linear**), whereas **AVL Trees**, **Binary Trees**, and **Graphs** are **non-linear** structures.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of swaps that can be performed in the Selection Sort algorithm?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **A) n − 1**

- **One Swap Per Outer Pass:** Selection Sort runs `n − 1` outer passes (`i = 0` to `n − 2`) and executes **at most `1` swap** (`A[i] ↔ A[min_idx]`) per pass, bounding total swaps at **`n − 1`** even though comparisons remain `n(n − 1)/2`.

questions.question: Which of the following has search efficiency of O(1)?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **C) Hash Table**

- **Direct Address Calculation:** A **Hash Table** computes bucket index `h(k)` in constant time, delivering **`O(1)` average-case** lookup (`O(1 + α)`), whereas balanced BSTs take `O(log n)` and heaps/linked lists take `O(n)` for arbitrary search.

questions.question: MST full form is ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **C) Minimum Spanning Tree**

- **Definition:** In a connected, undirected weighted graph `G = (V, E)`, an **MST (Minimum Spanning Tree)** spans all `|V|` vertices using `|V| − 1` acyclic edges with the **minimum total edge weight** (computed via **Prim's** or **Kruskal's** algorithm).

questions.question: If the array is already sorted, which of these algorithms will exhibit the best performance?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) Insertion Sort**

- **Adaptive `O(n)` Best Case:** On an already sorted array, **Insertion Sort** checks `A[i − 1] ≤ A[i]` once per pass with `0` shifts, finishing in **`Θ(n)`** linear time — outperforming Merge Sort (`Θ(n log n)`), Heap Sort (`Θ(n log n)`), and naive Quick Sort (`Θ(n²)`).

questions.question: What is the maximum number of swaps that can be performed in the Bubble Sort algorithm?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **D) n(n − 1)/2**

- **Maximum Inversion Count:** Every adjacent Bubble Sort swap eliminates exactly `1` inversion; a strictly reverse-sorted array contains `(n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 =` **`n(n − 1) / 2`** inversions, requiring `n(n − 1)/2` swaps.

questions.question: The main measures of the efficiency of an algorithm are ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **A) Time and space complexity**

- **Hardware-Independent Metrics:** Algorithm efficiency is evaluated along two primary axes as input size `n` grows: **time complexity** (count of elementary CPU steps) and **space complexity** (working memory footprint).

questions.question: If several elements are competing for the same bucket in the hash table, what is it called?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **C) Collision**

- **Same-Slot Contention:** When two or more distinct keys `k₁ ≠ k₂` evaluate to the identical bucket index `h(k₁) == h(k₂)` in a hash table, a **hash collision** occurs, which is resolved via **separate chaining** or **open addressing** (`linear/quadratic probing` or `double hashing`).

questions.question: Quick Sort algorithm is a ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **C) Divide & Conquer Algorithm**

- **Partition-and-Recurse:** **Quick Sort** selects a `pivot`, **divides** the subarray in-place into keys `≤ pivot` and `> pivot`, and **conquers** both partitions recursively (`T(n) = T(k) + T(n − k − 1) + Θ(n)`), requiring zero combine overhead.

questions.question: Name of the data structure used by recursion is ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **A) Stack**

- **LIFO Call-Stack Frames:** Every recursive invocation pushes a new **activation record** (parameters, local variables, return address) onto the runtime **call stack**, and each `return` pops the most recent frame in **LIFO** order.

questions.question: DAG full form is ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) Direct Acyclic Graph**

- **Standard Expansion:** Printed in the option list as *Direct Acyclic Graph* (canonically **Directed Acyclic Graph**), a **DAG** is a directed graph with **zero directed cycles**, enabling topological ordering, task dependency resolution, and linear-time shortest paths.
questions.sourceNote: The scan prints “Direct Acyclic Graph”; normalized explanation notes the standard term “Directed Acyclic Graph”.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm is known as ______.
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **D) Single Source shortest path**

- **SSSP Classification:** **Dijkstra's algorithm** computes minimum-weight paths from **one designated source vertex `s`** to all reachable vertices (`w(u, v) ≥ 0`), whereas **Floyd–Warshall** solves the All-Pairs Shortest Path (`APSP`) problem (**A**).

questions.question: Which of the following is true?

options.text: Prim's algorithm initializes with a vertex
Prim's algorithm initializes with an edge
Prim's algorithm initializes with a vertex which has smallest edge
Prim's algorithm initializes with a forest

questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **A) Prim's algorithm initializes with a vertex**

- **Vertex-Centric MST Growth:** **Prim's algorithm** starts from any **single arbitrary vertex `r`** (`key[r] = 0`) and grows one connected tree by repeatedly attaching the minimum-weight cut edge, whereas **Kruskal's** starts from a forest (**D**).

questions.question: Which of the following algorithms are used to find the shortest path from a source node to all other nodes in a weighted graph?
questions.answer:
**Correct Option:** **B) Dijkstra's Algorithm**

- **Weighted SSSP Solver:** **Dijkstra's algorithm** relaxes non-negative weighted edges using a min-priority queue (`O((V + E) log V)`), whereas **BFS** (**A**) works only on unweighted graphs and **Prim's/Kruskal's** (**C, D**) build Minimum Spanning Trees.

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: a.i) 2 marks + a.ii) 2 marks + b.i) 2 marks + b.ii) 2 marks

### a.i) What is an Algorithm? [2 Marks]

An **algorithm** is a finite, ordered sequence of definite (unambiguous) and effective computational instructions that transforms zero or more well-defined **inputs** into at least one desired **output** and **terminates** in finite steps.

### a.ii) Big-Oh (`O`) Asymptotic Notation [2 Marks]

- **Formal Definition:** A function `f(n)` belongs to **`O(g(n))`** (*asymptotic upper bound*) iff there exist positive constants `c > 0` and `n₀ ≥ 1` such that:
  `0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c · g(n)` for all `n ≥ n₀`.
- **Meaning & Example:** `f(n)` grows **no faster than** `g(n)` for sufficiently large inputs. For `f(n) = 4n² + 7n + 2`, choosing `c = 13` and `n₀ = 1` gives `4n² + 7n + 2 ≤ 13n²` → **`f(n) = O(n²)`**.

### b.i) What is Time Complexity? [2 Marks]

**Time complexity** `T(n)` is a hardware-independent measure of the **number of elementary operations** (comparisons, assignments, arithmetic steps) executed by an algorithm expressed as an asymptotic function of **input size `n`** across best, average, and worst cases.

### b.ii) Why Time and Space Complexities Are Important [2 Marks]

1. **Scalability Prediction:** Reveals whether an algorithm remains practical as `n` scales from `10³` to `10⁷` (`O(n log n)` finishes in milliseconds while `O(n²)` times out).
2. **Machine-Independent Comparison:** Ranks algorithms objectively regardless of CPU clock speed, OS, or compiler.
3. **Resource & Time–Space Trade-Offs:** Guides engineering choices under RAM/cache budgets (e.g., `O(1)`-space Heap Sort vs `O(n)`-space stable Merge Sort, or `O(n)` hash tables trading memory for `O(1)` lookup).

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 marks + b) 4 marks

### a) Time Complexity Derivation of the Doubling `while` Loop [4 Marks]

Given `i = 1; while (i <= n) { printf("CST\n"); i = i * 2; }`, variable `i` **doubles (`× 2`)** on every iteration rather than incrementing by `1`:

| Iteration # | Value of `i` Tested (`i ≤ n`) | Exponential Form | Next `i = i * 2` |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `1` | `1` | `2⁰` | `2¹` |
| `2` | `2` | `2¹` | `2²` |
| `3` | `4` | `2²` | `2³` |
| `…` | `…` | `…` | `…` |
| `k + 1` | `2^k ≤ n` | `2^k` | `2^(k+1) > n` *(terminates)* |

- **Solving Stopping Condition `2^k ≤ n < 2^(k+1)`:** Taking `log₂` across both sides gives `k ≤ log₂ n < k + 1`, so `k = ⌊log₂ n⌋` (e.g., for `n = 16`, `i` takes values `1, 2, 4, 8, 16` = `⌊log₂ 16⌋ + 1 = 5` iterations before `32 > 16` halts).
- **Total Iterations:** `k + 1 = ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1` (`O(1)` `printf` + multiplication work per iteration) → **Time Complexity = `Θ(log n)`** (or **`O(log n)`**), Auxiliary Space = **`O(1)`**.

### b) Basic Concept of the Divide and Conquer Algorithmic Model [4 Marks]

**Divide and Conquer (`D&C`)** decomposes a problem of size `n` recursively in three distinct stages:
1. **Divide:** Partition the input into `a ≥ 1` smaller, **independent** subproblems of size `n / b`.
2. **Conquer:** Solve the subproblems recursively (solving small base cases directly in `O(1)`).
3. **Combine:** Merge the subproblem answers to form the solution to the original problem.
- **Master Recurrence:** **`T(n) = a · T(n / b) + f(n)`**, where `f(n)` is the cost of dividing + combining.
- **Canonical Examples:** **Merge Sort** (`2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n)`), **Quick Sort** (`Θ(n log n)` average), and **Binary Search** (`T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n)`).

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 2 marks + b.i) 4 marks + b.ii) 2 marks

### a) Conditions When Linear Search Should Be Considered [2 Marks]

1. **Unsorted Data:** Input array is unordered and no prior sort index exists.
2. **Sequential-Access Structures:** Data resides in a **singly/doubly linked list** or input stream lacking `O(1)` random indexing.
3. **Small `n` or Single Query:** Dataset is tiny (`n ≲ 32`, cache-line scan beats branch overhead) or searched only once (where sorting first in `Θ(n log n)` would cost more than one `O(n)` scan).

### b.i) Algorithm for Binary Search (`A[0..n−1]` Sorted Ascending) [4 Marks]

```text
BINARY_SEARCH(A, n, key):
  low <- 0
  high <- n - 1
  while low <= high do
      mid <- low + floor((high - low) / 2)
      if A[mid] == key then
          return mid            // Match found at index mid
      else if A[mid] < key then
          low <- mid + 1        // Search upper half
      else
          high <- mid - 1       // Search lower half
  return -1                     // Key absent
```

### b.ii) Why Binary Search Complexity Is `O(log n)` [2 Marks]

- **Active Range Halving:** Initially `n` elements are active. After comparison `1`, at most `⌊n/2⌋` remain; after comparison `2`, at most `⌊n/2²⌋`; after comparison `k`, at most **`⌊n / 2^k⌋`** elements remain.
- **Worst-Case Bound:** The search terminates no later than when the active range shrinks below `1` element (`n / 2^k < 1 ⇒ 2^k > n ⇒ k > log₂ n`), requiring at most **`⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 = O(log n)`** comparisons (`T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)`) and **`O(1)`** extra space (for `n = 1,024`, at most `11` comparisons vs `1,024` in Linear Search).

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 marks + b) 4 marks

### a) Significance & Advantages of Height-Balancing a Binary Search Tree [4 Marks]

Every BST operation (`SEARCH`, `INSERT`, `DELETE`, `MIN`, `SUCCESSOR`) runs in **`O(h)`** time proportional to tree height `h`:
- **Degenerate Unbalanced Hazard:** Inserting sorted or nearly sorted keys (`10, 20, 30, 40`) into an ordinary BST produces a skewed chain of height **`h = n − 1`**, degrading all operations to **`O(n)`** linear search.
- **Height-Balance Invariant (`AVL` / `Red-Black`):** Maintaining **`|BF(x)| = |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1`** via `O(1)` local rotations (`LL, RR, LR, RL`) keeps tree height strictly bounded at **`h ≤ 1.44 log₂(n + 2) = Θ(log n)`**.

> [!COMPARE] Unbalanced BST vs Height-Balanced BST (AVL)
> | Parameter | Unbalanced BST | Height-Balanced BST (AVL) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Worst-Case Height `h`** | `n − 1` (`Θ(n)` skewed chain) | **`Θ(log n)`** |
> | **Worst-Case Search / Insert / Delete** | **`O(n)`** | **`O(log n)`** guaranteed |
> | **Predictable Real-Time Latency** | Vulnerable to sorted-input spikes | Deterministic logarithmic bound |

### b) Pseudocode of `INSERT` Operation in a Binary Search Tree [4 Marks]

```text
BST_INSERT(root, key):
  if root == NULL then
      return NEW_NODE(key)                    // Attach new leaf node
  if key < root.key then
      root.left <- BST_INSERT(root.left, key) // Branch into left subtree
  else if key > root.key then
      root.right <- BST_INSERT(root.right, key) // Branch into right subtree
  // (Duplicate keys ignored or handled per policy)
  return root
```

- **Complexity:** Traverses a single root-to-leaf path in **`O(h)`** time (`O(log n)` on a height-balanced AVL/Red-Black BST vs `O(n)` worst-case on a skewed BST) and `O(h)` recursion stack (`O(1)` if implemented iteratively).

b) Construct a minimum spanning tree from the given weighted graph using Kruskal’s algorithm.

subparts.label: b

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 3 marks + b) 5 marks

### a) How Prim's Algorithm Works [3 Marks]

**Prim's greedy MST algorithm** grows a **single connected tree `T`** vertex-by-vertex in `O(E log V)` time:
1. **Initialize:** Pick any start vertex `r`, set `key[r] = 0`, `key[v] = ∞` (`∀ v ≠ r`), and place all vertices in Min-Priority Queue `Q`.
2. **Greedy Cut Step:** Extract vertex `u` with minimum `key[u]` from `Q` (adding edge `(parent[u], u)` to the MST).
3. **Update Frontier:** For every neighbor `v ∈ Adj[u]` still in `Q`, if `w(u, v) < key[v]`, set `key[v] ← w(u, v)` and `parent[v] ← u`. Repeat until `Q = ∅` (`|V| − 1` edges added).

### b) Kruskal's MST Construction on the Given Weighted Graph (`|V| = 5`) [5 Marks]

**Printed Graph (`V = {A, B, C, D, E}`, `7` edges):** `A–B(1)`, `D–E(2)`, `B–C(3)`, `C–D(4)`, `A–E(5)`, `A–C(7)`, `A–D(10)`. **Kruskal's algorithm** sorts edges in ascending weight order and adds each edge iff `FIND(u) ≠ FIND(v)` (no cycle), stopping at `|V| − 1 = 4` edges:

| Step | Sorted Edge | Weight | Disjoint-Set Components Check | Decision | MST Edges |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **1** | **`A – B`** | `1` | `{A} ≠ {B}` → merge `{A, B}` | **Accept** | `1` |
| **2** | **`D – E`** | `2` | `{D} ≠ {E}` → merge `{D, E}` | **Accept** | `2` |
| **3** | **`B – C`** | `3` | `{A, B} ≠ {C}` → merge `{A, B, C}` | **Accept** | `3` |
| **4** | **`C – D`** | `4` | `{A, B, C} ≠ {D, E}` → merge `{A,B,C,D,E}` | **Accept (Stop!)** | **`4 = ¦V¦ − 1`** |
| `5` | `A – E` | `5` | Both in `{A,B,C,D,E}` (`A–B–C–D–E–A`) | *Reject (Cycle)* | `4` |
| `6` | `A – C` | `7` | Both in `{A,B,C,D,E}` (`A–B–C–A`) | *Reject (Cycle)* | `4` |
| `7` | `A – D` | `10` | Both in `{A,B,C,D,E}` (`A–B–C–D–A`) | *Reject (Cycle)* | `4` |

```ascii
  (A)---1---(B)---3---(C)---4---(D)---2---(E)    <-- Resulting MST Chain
```

- **Minimum Spanning Tree Cost:** `1 + 2 + 3 + 4 =` **`10`**.

questions.question: a) Explain Merge sort algorithm with suitable example.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Explain Merge sort algorithm with suitable example.

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: Algorithm & Merge Logic (3m) + Complete Split-and-Merge Trace (3m) + Complexity & Properties (2m)

### 1. Principle & Pseudocode of Merge Sort [3 Marks]

**Merge Sort** is a canonical **Divide and Conquer** sorting algorithm: (1) **Divide** `A[left..right]` at `mid = ⌊(left + right)/2⌋`; (2) **Conquer** both halves recursively; (3) **Combine** the two sorted halves in `Θ(n)` linear time using two-finger `MERGE`:

```text
MERGE_SORT(A, left, right):
  if left < right then
      mid <- left + floor((right - left) / 2)
      MERGE_SORT(A, left, mid)
      MERGE_SORT(A, mid + 1, right)
      MERGE(A, left, mid, right)

MERGE(A, left, mid, right):
  Copy A[left..mid] -> L[0..n1-1] and A[mid+1..right] -> R[0..n2-1]
  i <- 0;  j <- 0;  k <- left
  while i < n1 and j < n2 do
      if L[i] <= R[j] then A[k++] <- L[i++]   // '<=' preserves stability
      else                 A[k++] <- R[j++]
  Copy any remaining elements of L[] or R[] into A[k..right]
```

### 2. Worked Example on `A = [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]` (`n = 7`) [3 Marks]

```ascii
                 [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]
                 /                        \
        [38, 27, 43, 3]                [9, 82, 10]          <-- Divide
          /          \                   /      \
     [38, 27]      [43, 3]           [9, 82]    [10]
      /    \        /    \            /    \      |
   [38]   [27]   [43]    [3]        [9]   [82]  [10]        <-- Base (size 1)
      \    /        \    /            \    /      |
     [27, 38]      [3, 43]           [9, 82]    [10]        <-- Merge Level 1
          \          /                   \      /
        [3, 27, 38, 43]                [9, 10, 82]          <-- Merge Level 2
                 \                        /
                 [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]                 <-- Final Sorted
```

### 3. Complexity & Key Properties [2 Marks]

- **Recurrence & Time Complexity:** `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n)` (`log₂ n` recursion levels × `Θ(n)` merge cost per level) = **`Θ(n log n)`** in **Best, Average, and Worst cases**.
- **Space & Stability:** Requires **`Θ(n)`** auxiliary buffer for `L[]`/`R[]` (not in-place); **Stable** (`L[i] <= R[j]` keeps equal keys in original input order); ideal for **external sorting** and sorting **linked lists** (`O(1)` extra pointer space).

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 2 marks + b) 6 marks ### a) What is Hashing? [2 Marks] **Hashing** is a direct key-to-address mapping technique that uses a deterministic **hash function `h(k)`** (e.g., `h(k) = k mod m`) to translate key `k` into bucket index `0..m−1` of a **hash table `T`**, providing **`O(1)` expected-time** search, insertion, and deletion. ### b) Major Collision Resolution Techniques [6 Marks] When `k₁ ≠ k₂` map to the same index (`h(k₁) == h(k₂)`), collisions are resolved by two families of methods: > [!COMPARE] Separate Chaining vs Open Addressing Schemes > | Parameter | Separate Chaining (*Open Hashing*) | Open Addressing (*Linear / Quadratic / Double*) | > |---|---|---| > | **Storage Layout** | Slot `T[i]` heads a **linked list** of colliding keys. | All keys stored **directly inside array `T[0..m−1]`** (`α ≤ 1`). | > | **Probe Formula** | Traverse chain `T[h(k)]` (`O(1 + α)` expected). | **Linear:** `(h(k) + i) mod m`
**Quadratic:** `(h(k) + c₁i + c₂i²) mod m`
**Double Hashing:** `(h₁(k) + i·h₂(k)) mod m` | > | **Clustering & Deletion** | Zero primary clustering; direct node removal. | Linear has *primary clustering*, Quadratic *secondary*, Double *none*; requires `DELETED` tombstones. | - **Worked Mini-Comparison (`m = 7`, `h₁(k) = k mod 7`, keys `50, 700, 76, 85`):** - `50 → 1`, `700 → 0`, `76 → 6`. Now `85 mod 7 = 1` (**collides with `50` at slot `1`**): - **Separate Chaining:** Appends `85` to chain `T[1]: [50 → 85]`. - **Linear Probing:** Probes `(1 + 1) mod 7 =` **slot `2`**. - **Double Hashing (`h₂(k) = 5 − (k mod 5)`):** `h₂(85) = 5` → probes `(1 + 1·5) mod 7 = 6` (*occupied by `76`*), then `(1 + 2·5) mod 7 =` **slot `4`**. - **Rehashing:** When `α` exceeds threshold (`~0.75`), allocate a `~2×` prime-sized table and re-insert all keys in `O(n)`.

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 5 marks + b) 3 marks

### a) Dijkstra's Single-Source Shortest-Path (`SSSP`) Algorithm [5 Marks]

Precondition: Weighted graph `G = (V, E)` with **non-negative edge weights (`w(u, v) ≥ 0`)** and source `s`:

```text
DIJKSTRA(G, w, s):
  for each vertex v in G.V do
      dist[v] <- INFINITY
      parent[v] <- NIL
  dist[s] <- 0
  S <- EMPTY_SET                         // Settled vertices
  Q <- BUILD_MIN_HEAP(G.V)               // Priority queue keyed by dist[v]
  while Q is not empty do
      u <- EXTRACT_MIN(Q)                // Greedily pick closest unsettled u
      S <- S U {u}
      for each edge (u, v) in Adj[u] do  // Edge relaxation
          if dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v] then
              dist[v] <- dist[u] + w(u, v)
              parent[v] <- u
              DECREASE_KEY(Q, v, dist[v])
```

- **Complexity:** **`O((V + E) log V)`** with binary min-heap (`O(V²)` with simple array); **fails on negative edge weights** because settled vertices cannot be re-opened.

### b) Worked Step-by-Step Example (`s = A`) [3 Marks]

Directed weighted graph: `A→B(10)`, `A→C(3)`, `C→B(4)`, `C→D(8)`, `C→E(2)`, `B→D(2)`, `E→D(9)`:

| Step | Extracted `u` | `dist[A]` | `dist[B]` | `dist[C]` | `dist[D]` | `dist[E]` | Relaxations Performed |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| Init | — | **`0`** | `∞` | `∞` | `∞` | `∞` | — |
| **1** | **`A`** | `0` | `10` | **`3`** | `∞` | `∞` | `A→B(10)`, `A→C(3)` |
| **2** | **`C`** | `0` | `7` | `3` | `11` | **`5`** | `C→B(3+4=7<10)`, `C→D(11)`, `C→E(5)` |
| **3** | **`E`** | `0` | **`7`** | `3` | `11` | `5` | `E→D(5+9=14 > 11` unchanged) |
| **4** | **`B`** | `0` | `7` | `3` | **`9`** | `5` | `B→D(7+2=9 < 11)` |
| **5** | **`D`** | `0` | `7` | `3` | `9` | `5` | Final: `A:0, C:3, E:5, B:7, D:9` |

- **Reconstructed Shortest Paths from `A`:** `A → C` (`3`), `A → C → E` (`5`), `A → C → B` (`7`, beating direct `A → B = 10`), and `A → C → B → D` (`9`, beating `A → C → D = 11`).

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 6 marks + b) 2 marks

### a) Rabin–Karp String-Matching Algorithm [6 Marks]

Given text `T[0..n−1]`, pattern `P[0..m−1]`, alphabet radix `d` (e.g., `d = 256` for ASCII), and prime modulus `q`, **Rabin–Karp** slides an `O(1)` **modular rolling hash** across `T`:

```text
RABIN_KARP_MATCHER(T, P, d, q):
  n <- length(T);  m <- length(P)
  h <- d^(m - 1) mod q                   // Weight of leading digit
  p <- 0;  t0 <- 0
  for i <- 0 to m - 1 do                 // Horner preprocessing in Theta(m)
      p  <- (d * p  + P[i]) mod q
      t0 <- (d * t0 + T[i]) mod q
  for s <- 0 to n - m do                 // Slide window across text
      if p == ts then                    // Hash hit: verify characters!
          if P[0..m-1] == T[s..s+m-1] then
              print "Pattern occurs with shift", s
      if s < n - m then                  // O(1) rolling update for next shift
          ts+1 <- (d * (ts - T[s] * h) + T[s + m]) mod q
          if ts+1 < 0 then ts+1 <- ts+1 + q
```

- **Spurious-Hit Verification:** Because two unequal substrings can collide modulo `q` (`ts == p` while `T[s..s+m−1] ≠ P`), exact character comparison is mandatory on hash equality.
- **Worked Mini-Trace (`T = "2359023141526739921"`, `P = "31415"`, `d = 10`, `q = 13`):** `p = 31415 mod 13 = 7`. Window `"67399"` gives `67399 mod 13 = 7` (*spurious hit*, rejected on char check), while window **`"31415"` at `s = 6`** gives `7 == 7` and verifies as an **exact match**!

### b) Rabin–Karp vs Knuth–Morris–Pratt (`KMP`) [2 Marks]

> [!COMPARE] Rabin–Karp vs KMP String Matching
> | Parameter | Rabin–Karp Algorithm | KMP Algorithm |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Core Mechanism** | Modular **rolling hash** filtering + char verification. | Pattern **`LPS` prefix-function** state transitions (`0` text backtracking). |
> | **Preprocessing / Search Time** | `Θ(m)` / **`O(n + m)` average**, `O(n · m)` worst case (spurious hits). | `Θ(m)` / **`Θ(n + m)` deterministic worst case** (zero hash collisions). |
> | **Best Use Case** | **Multi-pattern** search, plagiarism detection, 2D matching. | Guaranteed linear-time **single-pattern** streaming search. |
